BSD (Basic Symmetry Detection) discards a newly generated state when another state was already reached with the same end vertex and the same set of used vertices (for snake problems: used vertices plus their neighbours) by a path at least as long. Both states can be extended in exactly the same ways, so only one needs to be searched. BSD helps only where many different paths lead to the same state.

BSD never makes the search worse and doesn't change the answer: no cell needs more expansions with BSD, and all 18,003 solutions found with BSD (1,506 instance-and-direction groups) have the same optimal path length as the runs without BSD and as DFBnB / IDA*.

It helps a lot on grids, a little on mazes, and almost not at all on the cube: about 40% fewer expansions for XA* on grids (up to 79% on a single cell), 3-13% on mazes, and at most about 1% on average on the cube (one outlier at 21%).

The more alternative routes a graph has, the more BSD saves (Tables 2 and 3). Larger and more open grids have many different paths to the same state, so savings grow with grid size and shrink as more cells are blocked. Mazes show this most clearly: with 0 open diamonds there is exactly one route between any two cells and BSD has no effect; each open diamond adds a loop and the saving grows with it.

XA* gains the most on grids. BiXA* only removes a state when both its forward and backward halves repeat a state seen before, which happens less often. On mazes the order flips and BiXA* gains more than XA*.
Lookahead makes no difference: BSD's saving is the same at every lookahead (e.g. XA* saves 40% on LSP grids at all six lookaheads). XMM's results barely depend on lookahead in the first place.

Time savings follow expansion savings, with two adjustments. (1) The 2026_10_11 runs were 5-9% faster overall: DFBnB and IDA* were re-run with exactly the same expansions but took less time (control rows in Table 1), so that much of every time saving isn't due to BSD. (2) XMM saves more time than expansions because it checks for duplicates right after creating a successor, before computing its heuristic, so every discarded duplicate also skips a heuristic computation. XA* computes the heuristic during the lookahead, before the duplicate check, so its time saving matches its expansion saving.
BSD solved runs that ran out of memory without it: XMM on the 8x8 LSP grid at 8% blocked now finishes at every lookahead, and XA* on the maze with 2 open diamonds now finishes at lookahead 1.

Still unresolved: no 7d cube run finished with or without BSD. The maze XMM+BSD cells with 2 open diamonds aren't in the tables: they ran out of memory without BSD, and the BSD runs have no job log to say what happened.

Each grid or maze cell is an average over 10 instances; each cell with BSD is compared with the same cell without BSD. Tables use the geometric mean over every lookahead, blocking level and grid size where both runs finished. CIB covers dimensions 4-6 and includes both the Finding and Proving columns.
Expansions are deterministic, so they measure BSD's effect cleanly (DFBnB and IDA* reproduced exactly the same expansions in both folders). Times also include machine noise.

The XMM BSD fix was committed on 5 Oct at 12:07 and the first BSD jobs started at 12:21, so the cluster very likely ran the fixed version (assuming the code was pulled before the jobs started). On LSP domains the fix makes no difference anyway: two states with the same end vertex and the same set of used vertices always have the same path length.
